entries.claim: Statistical power is the probability of rejecting a false null, equal to 1 minus the Type II error rate beta
entries.locator: NIST/SEMATECH, power and Type II error
entries.notes: Power rises with effect size, sample size and alpha

entries.claim: Cohen's benchmark conventions are d = 0.2/0.5/0.8 and r = 0.1/0.3/0.5 for small/medium/large effects, with 0.80 power as a common target
entries.locator: Cohen (1988); conventions restated in later reviews
entries.notes: Conventions are reference scales, not universal thresholds

entries.claim: A review of neuroscience literature estimated median statistical power near 21%
entries.locator: Button et al. (2013), Nat Rev Neurosci
entries.notes: Reported as an estimate for that literature, not all fields

entries.claim: For a two-sample mean comparison the per-group sample size is approximately 2(z_{1-alpha/2}+z_{1-beta})^2/d^2, about 15.7/d^2 at alpha 0.05 and power 0.80
entries.notes: Normal approximation; exact noncentral-t values are slightly larger

entries.claim: Required per-group n at alpha 0.05, two-sided, power 0.80 is about 394, 64 and 26 for d = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8
entries.notes: Common textbook/power-software values; normal approximation gives 392/63/25

entries.claim: Observed (post-hoc) power is a function of the p-value and sample size and should not replace a priori power analysis
entries.locator: discussion of low power and inflated effects
entries.notes: Winner's curse inflates effect sizes estimated from small samples

entries.claim: Interactive two-sample power from the normal approximation Phi(lambda - z) + Phi(-lambda - z)
entries.notes: Slightly overstates power in small samples; teaching use
